the following factors are important for reducing P excretion by poultry: 1) use of high-quality animal protein feeds; 2) selection of P supplements with the highest biological availability; 3) use of microbial phytase enzymes; and 4) judicious selection of the dietary P level.

the use of microbial phytases in diets for broilers and laying hens can be used to reduce the P content of the diet and the P concentration of the excreta, without compromising performance, and that the reduction in P content and P excretion is greater when the diets contain high amounts of phytate-P.

the use of phytases, the selection of high biological value P sources, the use of high quality animal protein meals, and the use of vitamin D isomers can all contribute to a reduction in dietary P requirements and fecal P excretion.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the nutritionist can reduce the dietary P levels and fecal excretions without adversely affecting the performance of growing poultry, provided that a quality control program is in place, and that the dietary P level is reduced in conjunction with a reduction in the phytate and/or nonphytate portion of the diet, and the use of a high biological value P supplement.
there is no simple answer to the question of how to reduce P in poultry diets.
the nutritionist must be aware of the potential for reducing P in poultry diets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the nutritionist has the responsibility of developing and implementing strategies to reduce the P content of poultry diets to the extent that the environmental and economic costs are justified.

, in the future, nutritionists must work closely with the feed manufacturer to produce diets that contain a minimum of excess P while maintaining adequate levels of available P for optimum growth and production.
, with the proper selection of ingredients, the addition of phytase, and the use of a quality control program, it is possible to reduce the dietary P content of poultry feeds by 30 to 50%.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the nutritionist must be able to identify the source of the P and its bioavailability in order to make the best use of the available P in the diet and thus reduce the amount of P in the feces.
the use of phytases in combination with other strategies to reduce P excretion is an effective means of reducing dietary P requirements and thus reducing P in poultry manure.

the nutritionist must be aware of the potential for dietary P to contribute to the P pollution of surface waters and must take appropriate action to minimize the amount of P in the excreta of the birds under his or her care.
